Chapter 6. The Unpredictable Waves of Grief and the Search for Stability.
You know, there are days when the world almost feels normal again. The sun rises, your coffee brews, and outside, the city just goes on humming. In those moments, there’s this cautious hope—maybe, just maybe, the worst is over.
But grief? It’s never straightforward. It doesn’t move in a neat little line. It comes in waves—sometimes they’re gentle, barely noticeable, and other times, they crash over you out of nowhere.
Picture this: it’s a quiet afternoon, and you’re sorting through an old drawer. Suddenly, there it is—a photograph you forgot about. It’s so vivid, so full of life, that for a moment, it’s like time folds in on itself. Maybe you’re right back at the beach, laughter in the air, sand between your toes, someone’s warm hand in yours. That memory? It’s both a gift and a wound. And just like that, the tears come. The sense of loss hits just as sharply as ever.
Most people think grief fades with time, right? Like, it should get easier, softer, more manageable. But the truth is, it ebbs and flows. The smallest things—a song on the radio, the smell of a favorite meal, seeing a couple walking hand in hand—can trigger it all over again.
These moments might feel like setbacks, but really, they’re reminders. They show just how deep that love was.
Over time, you start to learn how to ride those waves. Stability, it turns out, isn’t about never feeling pain. It’s about moving through it, letting yourself feel it, and knowing you can make it out the other side. Some days, the ache is just a quiet hum in the background. Other days, it’s all you can hear. But little by little, you figure out how to navigate those shifts.
And here’s something important: small routines become your anchors. Maybe it’s a morning walk, a call with a friend, or just the simple ritual of making tea. These little acts—they don’t erase the pain, but they give you something to hold onto. They connect the past and the present, helping you find your footing when things feel shaky.
Healing isn’t about forgetting. It’s about weaving those memories into the fabric of your daily life. You carry them with you, not as a burden, but as part of who you are.
Eventually, it becomes clear—grief isn’t something you conquer. It’s something you learn to live with. You start to treat yourself with a little more gentleness, making space for both sorrow and joy. It’s a process, always ongoing—a dance between holding on and letting go.
